Caching & Prediction Stores#

PerformanceStatistical 1 min read
◆ The PatternDon't predict what you've already predicted

// Don't predict what you've already predicted

If 80% of your requests are repeated inputs (product recommendations, credit scores), a prediction cache (Redis, Memcached) can serve them in microseconds. Prediction stores precompute scores for all known entities on a schedule. TTL and invalidation strategies keep results fresh.

// Interactive — cache hit rate vs latency
Cache Hit Rate %70%
Avg Latency—
Pattern bridge: Prediction caching is memoization at system scale. In markets, precomputed support/resistance levels serve the same purpose — calculate once, reference many times.
Worked example

A million keys whose popularity follows Zipf’s law. Caching just the top 1% — 10,000 keys — serves 68% of requests. At 1 ms from cache and 50 ms from the model, the average falls to 16.7 ms. Skewed traffic is why small caches work so well.

Where it misleads
  • A cached prediction is only as fresh as its TTL; for fast-changing inputs a cache serves stale answers confidently.
  • If traffic is not skewed — every request unique — a cache adds cost and gains nothing.
  • Cache keys must include the model version, or a rollout keeps serving the old model’s answers.
In code
keys = 1_000_000
rank = np.arange(1, keys + 1)
share = (1 / rank) / (1 / rank).sum()             # Zipf: the k-th most popular key gets traffic ~ 1/k
hit_rate = share[: keys // 100].sum()             # cache the top 1% of keys
latency = hit_rate * 1 + (1 - hit_rate) * 50       # ms: 1 from cache, 50 from the model

Assumes import numpy as np and import pandas as pd. Each snippet carries its own example numbers; the comments say which are made up or simulated.

Sources
  • L. Breslau, P. Cao, L. Fan, G. Phillips & S. Shenker, “Web Caching and Zipf-like Distributions: Evidence and Implications”, IEEE INFOCOM, 1999
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications, M. Kleppmann, O’Reilly, 2017
